--- title: "Pandas Introduction" error: true --- ## Goals 1. Understand what `pandas` is for and when to reach for it. 2. Load a CSV file of tabular data into a Python session. 3. Meet the two core objects: the `Series` (one column) and the `DataFrame` (a full table). 4. Inspect a table using its attributes and a few summary methods. 5. Answer basic analytics questions with the following operations: selecting columns, sorting, filtering, and creating new columns. ## Overview - [`pandas`](https://pandas.pydata.org/) is a Python library for data analysis and manipulation. - It is built for **tabular data**: rows and columns, just like a spreadsheet or a database table. - It is the standard tool for this job in Python, so nearly every data analytics workflow you meet will use it. `pandas` has two main objects. | Name | Dimensions | Description | |----------------|------------|----------------------------------------------------| | `Series` | 1 | One labeled column of values, all of the same type | | `DataFrame` | 2 | A labeled table made up of several columns | ### What can `pandas` do? The library is huge. For now, we only need a small corner of it: - Reading and writing files (CSV, Excel, and more). - Looking at, sorting, and filtering tables. - Creating new columns from existing ones. ## Getting Started We must `import` the package like any other Python package. ::: {#ddaf2999 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import pandas as pd ``` ::: By convention, `pandas` is imported under the nickname `pd`. Nearly all tutorials, books, and Stack Overflow answers do the same, so you should too. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Where to learn more The official [Getting Started guide](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/index.html) and [User Guide](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/index.html) are good references. You are not expected to memorize functions; part of working with `pandas` is looking things up. ::: ## Loading your first dataset Suppose you have an advertising dataset: for each of 200 markets, the amount spent on TV, radio, and newspaper advertising (in thousands of dollars) and the resulting product sales (in thousands of units). It is stored as a CSV file (**C**omma-**S**eparated **V**alues), which is just plain text: ```{text} ,TV,radio,newspaper,sales 1,230.1,37.8,69.2,22.1 2,44.5,39.3,45.1,10.4 3,17.2,45.9,69.3,9.3 4,151.5,41.3,58.5,18.5 ``` - The first line holds the **column names**. - Each following line is one **row** of data, with values separated by commas. - The first column has no name; it holds row numbers (1, 2, 3, ...). We load it with `pd.read_csv`: ::: {#e51a9174 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Replace with the real path to the file on your computer or Colab session ad_data = pd.read_csv( os.path.join("assets", "ISLP_Advertising.csv"), index_col=0 ) ad_data ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
TV radio newspaper sales
1 230.1 37.8 69.2 22.1
2 44.5 39.3 45.1 10.4
3 17.2 45.9 69.3 9.3
4 151.5 41.3 58.5 18.5
5 180.8 10.8 58.4 12.9
... ... ... ... ...
196 38.2 3.7 13.8 7.6
197 94.2 4.9 8.1 9.7
198 177.0 9.3 6.4 12.8
199 283.6 42.0 66.2 25.5
200 232.1 8.6 8.7 13.4

200 rows × 4 columns

``` ::: ::: A few things to notice: - `os.path.join(...)` builds a file path that works on any operating system. - `index_col=0` says "use the first column (the row numbers) as the row labels instead of as ordinary data." - The result is stored in a variable, `ad_data`, so we can work with it. This dataset comes from Chapter 2 of *An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Python* (ISLP). - Each **row** is one market. - Each **column** is one variable (TV spend, radio spend, and so on). ### More on the `index` Every `pandas` object has an internal `index`, which is an immutable, 1D sequence used to store axis labels. This is how we can distinguish records from each other, even if they happen to contain the same values across every column. - Not every data file you work with will have an internal index. In such cases, `pandas` will create row labels automatically. - There is no need for `index` to be numbers. - If your dataset contains a column that can serve as a unique identifier, you can specify it with `index_col` when loading data. ## Other ways to read and write data `pandas` can read from and write to many formats. The most common pairs are: - `pd.read_csv` / `.to_csv` - `pd.read_excel` / `.to_excel` - `pd.read_sql` / `.to_sql` For example, `ad_data.to_csv("my_copy.csv")` saves a table back to a file. `pandas` can even read CSV text straight from a Python string if we wrap it in a `StringIO` object. This is handy for small examples: ::: {#529d4473 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from io import StringIO small = pd.read_csv(StringIO(""",TV,radio,newspaper,sales 1,230.1,37.8,69.2,22.1 2,44.5,39.3,45.1,10.4 3,17.2,45.9,69.3,9.3 4,151.5,41.3,58.5,18.5"""), index_col=0) small ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
TV radio newspaper sales
1 230.1 37.8 69.2 22.1
2 44.5 39.3 45.1 10.4
3 17.2 45.9 69.3 9.3
4 151.5 41.3 58.5 18.5
``` ::: ::: ## `Series` vs `DataFrame` - A `DataFrame` is a full table (like a whole Excel sheet). - A `Series` is a single column of that table (like the `sales` column). ::: {#bac8b2a1 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # whole table = DataFrame type(ad_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` pandas.DataFrame ``` ::: ::: ::: {#9e02281f .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # one column = Series sales = ad_data["sales"] type(sales) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` pandas.Series ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cf8b0e2d .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # peek at the first 5 values sales.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 1 22.1 2 10.4 3 9.3 4 18.5 5 12.9 Name: sales, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ### The `Series` A `Series` has two parts: the **values** and an **index** (the labels for each value). ::: {#f1867963 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Think of this as last week's daily website visits visits = pd.Series( [120, 135, 150, 145, 160, 170, 190], index=["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"] ) visits ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` Mon 120 Tue 135 Wed 150 Thu 145 Fri 160 Sat 170 Sun 190 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: - First input: a `list` of values. - Second input: the labels, given through the *named* argument `index`. - Bottom line of the output: `dtype` is the **data type** of the values (here `int64`, whole numbers). A `Series` holds one data type. We can pull out its parts and compute with it: ::: {#7d15e0cc .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} visits.values # the data ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` array([120, 135, 150, 145, 160, 170, 190]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#336e6ba8 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} visits.index # the labels ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` Index(['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun'], dtype='str') ``` ::: ::: ::: {#0c9fff0f .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} visits.mean() # average daily visits ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` np.float64(152.85714285714286) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#4474cfcb .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} visits["Fri"] # look up one value by label ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` np.int64(160) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#a756c787 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} visits.sort_values(ascending=False) # busiest days first ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` Sun 190 Sat 170 Fri 160 Wed 150 Thu 145 Tue 135 Mon 120 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: Arithmetic acts on every value at once ("vectorized"), so no loop is needed: ::: {#970a87da .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} visits * 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` Mon 240 Tue 270 Wed 300 Thu 290 Fri 320 Sat 340 Sun 380 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ### The `DataFrame` A `DataFrame` is a collection of `Series` that share the same row labels. It has: - an **index** (row labels), - **columns** (column names), and - **values** (the data). ## Attributes of a `DataFrame` *Attributes* are pieces of information stored on an object. Unlike methods, they are written **without parentheses**. ::: {#985dce39 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data.shape # (number of rows, number of columns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` (200, 4) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#ab98ed4d .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data.columns # column names ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` Index(['TV', 'radio', 'newspaper', 'sales'], dtype='str') ``` ::: ::: ::: {#f83d6214 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data.index # row labels ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` RangeIndex(start=1, stop=201, step=1) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#388d9fef .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data.dtypes # data type of each column ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` TV float64 radio float64 newspaper float64 sales float64 dtype: object ``` ::: ::: ::: {#983b5b45 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data.size # total number of cells (rows x columns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` 800 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Attribute vs. method `ad_data.shape` is an attribute (no parentheses). `ad_data.head()` is a method, i.e. a function attached to the object, so it needs parentheses. If you forget the parentheses on a method, Python shows you the method itself rather than running it. ::: ## Quick summaries ### Looking at the data ::: {#968287cb .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data.head() # first 5 rows ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ```{=html}
TV radio newspaper sales

``` ::: ::: ::: {#85dad8fb .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data.tail(3) # last 3 rows ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}

(Compare each non-null count to the number of rows.) ### Descriptive statistics ::: {#03148532 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data.describe() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ```{=html}

We can also compute one statistic for one column: ::: {#434d91bd .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data["sales"].mean() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ``` np.float64(14.0225) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#a254da3c .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data["sales"].median() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ``` np.float64(12.9) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#90fe691d .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data["sales"].max() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ``` np.float64(27.0) ``` ::: ::: ## Selecting columns Use square brackets and a column name to get a `Series`. Use a **list** of names to get a smaller `DataFrame`: ::: {#88482673 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data["TV"].head() # one column -> Series ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ``` 1 230.1 2 44.5 3 17.2 4 151.5 5 180.8 Name: TV, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#da1db5a4 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data[["TV", "sales"]].head() # list of columns -> DataFrame ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Note the double brackets in the second example: the outer pair means "select," and the inner pair is the Python list of names. ## Sorting and filtering ### Sorting: "Top markets by sales" ::: {#a6b0677b .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Sort by sales, highest first ad_data.sort_values("sales", ascending=False).head(10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ```{=html}

(Hint: change `ascending`.) ::: {.callout-note} `sort_values` returns a *new* sorted table; `ad_data` itself is not changed unless you assign the result to a variable. ::: ### Filtering: "Markets with high TV spend" Filtering uses a **condition** that produces `True`/`False` for each row. Only rows with `True` are kept. ::: {#0fbb3337 .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} ad_data["TV"] > 150 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ``` 1 True 2 False 3 False 4 True 5 True ... 196 False 197 False 198 True 199 True 200 True Name: TV, Length: 200, dtype: bool ``` ::: ::: ::: {#32c981e3 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} high_tv = ad_data[ad_data["TV"] > 150] high_tv ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ```{=html}

Are sales higher when total spend is above average?
